Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: As a data scientist, Alexandra's work was her solace. She threw herself into complex projects, pouring over lines of code and analyzing patterns in data that others might find mundane. It was a trait that had served her well throughout her career, but lately, it had become an essential coping mechanism. Alexandra's troubles began two years ago when she witnessed a devastating fire in an Arab village while visiting her husband's family abroad. The blaze had ravaged the community, leaving many homeless and injured. She recalled the sound of screams, the smell of smoke, and the sight of flames engulfing everything in their path. Those sensory details still haunted her. The memories lingered, but it wasn't until she returned to her daily routine that Alexandra realized how deeply they had affected her. Simple things like seeing flames on TV or walking past an Arab restaurant would transport her back to that day. She'd feel a jolt of fear and adrenaline as if the event was happening all over again. Over time, Alexandra found herself becoming increasingly withdrawn. She avoided social gatherings, fearing encounters with strangers who might somehow remind her of the traumatic event. At home, she became obsessed with checking door locks and windows, convinced that someone could break in at any moment. Her husband tried to be supportive, but Alexandra couldn't shake off the feeling of responsibility for not having protected others during the fire. She'd replay the events leading up to the tragedy, wondering if there was something she could've done differently. "Why didn't I react faster?" or "What if I had called for help sooner?" The self-blame gnawed at her, making her question whether her life was worth living. As Alexandra struggled with these thoughts, she turned to work as a distraction. Long hours in front of the computer became her norm, but even that coping mechanism began to fray. Her performance suffered, and colleagues started noticing changes in her demeanor. Despite this, Alexandra couldn't stop working; it was a never-ending attempt to outrun her memories. The stress took its toll on her marriage as well. Her husband felt helpless watching his wife become increasingly isolated, unable to connect with the woman he once knew. Their conversations became strained, and even small talk felt forced. One evening, Alexandra's computer froze while she was working late, forcing her to take a break. As she stepped away from the screen, she caught herself checking the locks again - a ritual that had become automatic. In that moment, something clicked; she realized she couldn't keep running. The strain on her marriage and her own well-being had finally pushed her to seek help. Alexandra made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to break free from the hold of those memories. She was uncertain about what lay ahead but knew she needed to confront the trauma head-on. For the first time in months, there was a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, she could learn to live alongside her memories instead of letting them define her. With trepidation and determination, Alexandra took that crucial step toward healing, leaving behind the relative safety of her work and confronting the darkness she'd been trying to outrun for so long.
